1.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Praise Yah, all people]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Praise God in his sanctuary and in his mighty heavens]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe an **expanse** that is characterized by **strength**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in his mighty expanse]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the expanse where he is mighty]

2.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Praise him for his mighty deeds; yes, praise him because he is so abundantly great]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **greatness** that is characterized by **abundance**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to how abundantly great he is]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **abundance** and **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because he is greater than any other thing]

3.note: A **shofar** is a musical instrument made from a ram’s horn. If your readers would not be familiar with what a **shofar** is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a ram’s-horn trumpet] or [a horn]

4.note: A tambourine is a musical instrument, a percussion instrument with a head like a drum that can be hit. It has pieces of metal around the side edges; they make a rattling sound when the instrument is shaken. Alternate translation: [with the sound of the tambourine]

5.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Praise him with all kinds of cymbals]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **cymbals** that are characterized by **hearing**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with cymbals that ring out clearly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hearing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with cymbals that can be clearly heard]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **cymbals** that are characterized by **a shout**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with cymbals that sound like a shout]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a shout**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that ring out loudly]

6.note: The psalmist is saying what he wants **all of the breath** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that all of the breath praise Yah]

Here, **all of the breath** represents all living creatures. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all living creatures]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Praise Yah, all people]

The words **Hallelu Yah** mean “praise Yahweh.” The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name Yahweh. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Praise Yah, that is, Yahweh]
